claims.text: The baseline material is a non-equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi-type high-entropy alloy with a single-phase solid solution.
Systematically changing constituent-element ratios is a method for tuning the properties of a high-entropy alloy.
Partial substitution of Fe with Mn is an example of the proposed composition-tuning method.
Changing constituent ratios will shift the Curie temperature.
Changing constituent ratios will shift the magnetocaloric response.
Composition variation will enhance magnetocaloric performance relative to the baseline alloy.
Elemental ratios, particularly Fe and Mn contents, can be varied through controlled doping during arc or induction melting followed by annealing.
Consistent melting and homogenization protocols can help isolate composition effects by maintaining comparable microstructures.
Partial elemental substitution changes the local chemical environment.
Partial elemental substitution alters magnetic-interaction pathways.
Adjusting elemental composition modifies the alloy's overall electron concentration.
Adjusting elemental composition modifies exchange interactions.
Changes in electron concentration and exchange interactions shift the magnetic transition temperature.
Shifting the magnetic transition temperature tunes the magnetocaloric response near the Curie region.
The intervention will produce a modest but discernible shift in Curie temperature.
The intervention will improve the peak magnetocaloric effect relative to the undoped reference alloy.
Doping should remain within the alloy's solubility range to suppress unwanted secondary phases.
Unwanted secondary phases may degrade magnetic or structural properties.
The quantitative Curie-temperature and magnetocaloric changes depend on phase stability and mixing effects.
